# Explicit Constructions of Finite Groups as Monodromy Groups

**Authors:** Ra-Zakee Muhammad, Javier Santiago and Eyob Tsegaye Address: Department of Mathematics, Pomona College, 333 N. College Way Claremont, CA 91711 Email address: rmab2018@mymail.pomona.edu Address: Department of Computer Science, University of Puerto Rico, Río Piedras, 17 Ave Universidad, Ste 1701, San Juan, Puerto Rico 00925-2537 Email address: javier.santiago16@upr.edu Address: Deparment of Mathematics, Stanford University, Building 380, Stanford, California 94305 Email address: etsegay@stanford.edu

## Abstract

In 1963, Greenberg proved that every finite group appears as the monodromy group of some morphism of Riemann surfaces. In this paper, we give two constructive proofs of Greenberg’s result. First, we utilize free groups, which given with the universal property and their construction as discrete subgroups of $\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{R})$ , yield a very natural realization of finite groups as monodromy groups. We also give a proof of Greenberg’s result based on triangle groups $\Delta(m,n,k)$ . Given any finite group $G$ , we make use of subgroups of $\Delta(m,n,k)$ in order to explicitly find a morphism $\pi$ such that $G\simeq\operatorname{Mon}(\pi)$ .

## 1. Introduction

Greenberg’s celebrated result [8] from 1963 shows than any finite group can be realized as the monodromy group of some morphism of Riemann surfaces. Over $40$ years later, in [13], Wolfart provided a method to make Greenberg’s ideas explicit for finite cyclic groups. Specifically, he utilizes surjections from triangle groups in order to construct the cyclic group as a monodromy group. Inspired by Wolfart, in this paper we seek to make Greenberg’s result explicit for all finite groups. That is, given any finite group $G$ , our goal is to find an explicit morphism $\pi$ with monodromy group $\operatorname{Mon}(\pi)$ such that $G\simeq\operatorname{Mon}(\pi)$ . On that account, we will be presenting two constructive proofs of Greenberg’s classical result.

We first present a natural construction arising from the theory of free groups, where we make use of the appearance of all groups $G$ as quotient groups of free groups [5], as well as the identification of the free group of rank $2$ with the congruence subgroup $\Gamma(2)$ [7]. Then we give a proof of our main result, which is a construction which utilizes surjections from appropriate subgroups of triangle groups. The formal construction is as follows:

#### Theorem 1.1.

Let $S_{n}$ be the symmetric group of degree $n$ and let $\varphi\colon\Delta(2,n,n-1)\to S_{n}$ be the homomorphism given by

$$ \gamma_{0}\mapsto(1\;2),\quad\gamma_{1}\mapsto(1\;2\;\cdots\;n),\quad\gamma_{\infty}\mapsto(n\;\cdots\;3\;2). $$

Then,

- (i) $\varphi$ is a surjective group homomorphism. Moreover, if $n<5$ , then $\varphi$ is an isomorphism.

- (ii) If $G$ is a subgroup of $S_{n}$ , then $\Gamma=\varphi^{-1}(G)$ and $\Gamma^{\prime}=\operatorname{ker}(\varphi)$ are both Fuchsian groups.

- (iii) $G\simeq\operatorname{Mon}(\pi)$ , where $\pi\colon\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash\mathbb{H}\to\Gamma\backslash\mathbb{H}$ is the canonical projection and $G$ , $\Gamma$ , and $\Gamma^{\prime}$ are as stated in (ii).

Note that by Cayley’s theorem, we may identify any finite group $G$ as a subgroup of $S_{n}$ for appropriate $n$ . The organization of the paper is the following. In Section 2, we define the concepts of Fuchsian groups and triangle groups, in addition to giving a description of monodromy in simple algebraic terms. Moreover, we also go into detail on the explicit constructions of free groups $F_{r}$ as subgroups of $\Gamma(2)$ . In Section 3, we then give both constructive proofs of Greenberg’s result.

## 2. Preliminaries

Recall $\operatorname{SL}_{2}(\mathbb{R})$ , as a topological space, can be naturally identified with a subset of $\mathbb{R}^{4}$ . Consequently, $\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{R})$ is endowed with a quotient topology. In this paper, we will be interested in subgroups $\Gamma\leq\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{R})$ such that the topology induced in $\Gamma$ is discrete.

#### Definition 2.1.

[7] A Fuchsian group is a subgroup $\Gamma\leq\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{R})$ such that for all $\gamma\in\Gamma$ there is a neighbourhood $V$ of $\gamma$ in $\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{R})$ with $V\cap\Gamma=\{\gamma\}$ .

By definition, it is clear that if $\Gamma$ is a Fuchsian group and $\Gamma^{\prime}\leq\Gamma$ , then $\Gamma^{\prime}$ is also a Fuchsian group. This will be relevant when working with subgroups of $\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{Z})$ , since $\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{Z})$ is a discrete subgroup of $\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{R})$ . For more details regarding Fuchsian groups, see [10, 9, 6].

As mentioned before, the goal of this paper is to explicitly realize any finite group $G$ as the monodromy group of some branched cover. Now, on one hand, given a branched cover of Riemann surfaces, we may realize the monodromy group by lifting paths around the branch points. However, we may also take an algebraic point of view. In [7], we see that monodromy groups can also be explicitly constructed from Fuchsian groups. Namely, given two Fuchsian groups $\Gamma^{\prime},\Gamma$ with $\Gamma^{\prime}\leq\Gamma$ , we have $\displaystyle{\frac{\Gamma}{\bigcap_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\gamma^{-1}\Gamma^{\prime}\gamma}\simeq\operatorname{Mon}(\pi)}$ , where $\pi\colon\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash\mathbb{H}\to\Gamma\backslash\mathbb{H}$ . Furthermore, $\displaystyle{\bigcap_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\gamma^{-1}\Gamma^{\prime}\gamma}$ is the largest normal subgroup of $\Gamma$ that is contained in $\Gamma^{\prime}$ (also called the normal core). Therefore, if $\Gamma^{\prime}$ is a normal subgroup of $\Gamma$ , we have the following simple description of $\operatorname{Mon}(\pi)$ .

#### Corollary 2.2.

[7, Corollary 2.59] Let $\Gamma^{\prime},\Gamma$ be Fuchsian groups. If $\Gamma^{\prime}\trianglelefteq\Gamma$ , then $\Gamma/\Gamma^{\prime}\simeq\operatorname{Mon}(\pi)$ , where $\pi\colon\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash\mathbb{H}\to\Gamma\backslash\mathbb{H}$ .

Making Greenberg’s result explicit is then a purely algebraic question: Given any finite group $G$ , can we find Fuchsian groups $\Gamma^{\prime},\Gamma$ with $\Gamma^{\prime}\trianglelefteq\Gamma$ such that $G\simeq\Gamma/\Gamma^{\prime}$ ? Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 1.1 provide two separate constructions that answer this question.

In Theorem 3.1, we take $\Gamma$ to be a free group, whose rank depends on the number of generators of the finite group $G$ . This construction is based on both the fact that $\Gamma(2)$ is a free group generated by $A=\pm\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix},B=\pm\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 2&1\end{bmatrix}\in\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{Z})$ [2], as well as the classical result that the free group of rank two contains freely generated subgroups of rank $r$ for any $r\in\mathbb{N}$ . The following lemma gives an explicit construction of free groups of rank $r$ as subgroups of $\Gamma(2)$ .

#### Lemma 2.3.

[4, Proposition 7.80] Let $A=\pm\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=\pm\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 2&1\end{bmatrix}$ and let $F_{r}=\langle\;B^{-j}AB^{j}\;|\;j=0,1,\dots,r-1\;\rangle$ . Then $F_{r}$ is a free subgroup of rank $r$ in $\Gamma(2)$ .

For Theorem 1.1 we choose $\Gamma$ to be a partiular subgroup of a triangle group.

#### Definition 2.4.

Let $m,n,k\in\mathbb{N}$ . Then a group with presentation

$$ \Delta(m,n,k)=\langle\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\gamma_{\infty}\;|\;\gamma_{0}^{m}=\gamma_{1}^{n}=\gamma_{\infty}^{k}=\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{\infty}=1\rangle $$

is called a triangle group.

An important result regarding triangle groups is the following:

#### Theorem 2.5.

[1] Let $m,n,k\in\mathbb{N}$ . Then the triangle group $\Delta(m,n,k)$ is a Fuchsian group.

#### Remark 2.6.

[7] Notice $\Gamma(2)$ can be identified with the triangle group $\Delta(\infty,\infty,\infty)$ .

In both Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 1.1, we will construct a surjective homomorphism $\varphi$ from $\Gamma$ onto the finite group $G$ , and $\operatorname{ker}(\varphi)$ will be the natural choice for the normal subgroup $\Gamma^{\prime}$ .

## 3. Constructions

In this section, we will be using Corollary 2.2 to explicitly realize finite groups $G$ as monodromy groups. As discussed in Section 2, given a finite group $G$ , our approach is to find a Fuchsian group $\Gamma$ and a surjective homomorphism $\varphi\colon\Gamma\to G$ such that $G\simeq\Gamma/\Gamma^{\prime}$ , where $\Gamma^{\prime}=\operatorname{ker}(\varphi)$ . The kernel of such a homomorphism $\varphi$ is then a normal Fuchsian subgroup of $\Gamma$ . As a result, we can then use Corollary 2.2 to conclude $G\simeq\operatorname{Mon}(\pi)$ , where $\pi\colon\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash\mathbb{H}\to\Gamma\backslash\mathbb{H}$ is the canonical map. Two separate constructions will be provided, one with free groups and one with subgroups of triangle groups.

### 3.1. Free group construction

From group theory, we have that any group $G$ is isomorphic to a quotient group of some free groups. Here, we will be using the structure of groups as quotients of free groups in order to explicitly express finite groups as monodromy groups.

Consider both $\Gamma(2)=\langle A,B\rangle$ and $F_{r}$ as constructed in Lemma 2.3.

#### Theorem 3.1.

Let $G$ be an $r$ -generated finite group, $\Gamma=F_{r}$ and $\varphi$ a surjective group homomorphism $\varphi\colon\Gamma\to G$ with $\Gamma^{\prime}=\ker\varphi$ . Then,

- (i) $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma^{\prime}$ are both Fuchsian groups. Moreover, $\Gamma^{\prime}$ is a free group of rank $1+\lvert G\rvert(r-1)$ .

- (ii) $G\simeq\operatorname{Mon}(\pi)$ , where $\pi\colon\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash\mathbb{H}\to\Gamma\backslash\mathbb{H}$ is the canonical projection.

#### Proof.

$(i)$ By the construction in Lemma 2.3, we see that $\Gamma\leq\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\mathbb{Z})$ , and thus, it is a Fuchsian group. Since $\Gamma^{\prime}=\operatorname{ker}(\varphi)$ is a subgroup of the Fuchsian group $\Gamma$ , it then follows that $\Gamma^{\prime}$ is also a Fuchsian group. Notice further, by the Schreier index formula [11], the rank of $\Gamma^{\prime}$ is $1+\lvert G\rvert(r-1)$ . $(ii)$ Since $\Gamma^{\prime},\Gamma$ are Fuchsian groups, we then have the canonical map between Riemann surfaces $\pi\colon\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash\mathbb{H}\to\Gamma\backslash\mathbb{H}$ . Consequently, given that $\varphi$ is surjective, we have $G\simeq\Gamma/\Gamma^{\prime}$ , and from Corollary 2.2 we can conclude $G\simeq\operatorname{Mon}(\pi)$ . ∎

#### Remark 3.2.

Given the group presentation for $G$ , then $\operatorname{ker}(\varphi)$ can be seen as smallest normal subgroup containing the relations in $G$ .

Recall that the free group $\Gamma(2)$ can be identified with the triangle group $\Delta(\infty,\infty,\infty)$ . Thus, in Theorem 3.1, we can view $\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}$ as subgroups of $\Delta(\infty,\infty,\infty)$ . We now give another proof of Greenberg’s result, this time using subgroups of the triangle group $\Delta(m,n,k)$ with $m,n,k$ finite.

### 3.2. Triangle group construction

The specific triangle group we will be working with is $\Delta(2,n,n-1)$ . As stated in Theorem 1.1, let

$$ \varphi\colon\Delta(2,n,n-1)\to S_{n} $$

be the homomorphism given by

$$ \gamma_{0}\mapsto(1\;2),\quad\gamma_{1}\mapsto(1\;2\;\cdots\;n),\quad\gamma_{\infty}\mapsto(n\;\cdots\;3\;2). $$

#### Proof of Theorem 1.1.

$(i)$ Since $S_{n}$ is generated by the transposition $(1\textbf{ }2)$ and the $n$ -cycle $(1\textbf{ }2\textbf{ }\cdots\text{ }n)$ and these are mapped to by $\gamma_{0}$ and $\gamma_{1}$ respectively, $\varphi$ is a surjective map. Now, notice if $n\geq 5$ , then $\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{n}+\frac{1}{n-1}<1$ . In that case, $\Delta(2,n,n-1)$ corresponds to a tiling of the hyperbolic plane. And so, it follows that $\Delta(2,n,n-1)$ is an infinite group [12]. For the cases with $n<5$ we go one by one. If $n=2$ , then $\Delta(2,2,1)$ is the cyclic group $C_{2}\simeq S_{2}$ . If $n=3$ , then $\Delta(2,3,2)$ is the dihedral group $D_{3}\simeq S_{3}$ . And finally, if $n=4$ , then $\Delta(2,4,3)$ is the octahedral group, which is isomorphic to $S_{4}$ [3]. $(ii)$ Since $\Gamma=\varphi^{-1}(G)$ and $\Gamma^{\prime}=\operatorname{ker}(\varphi)$ are subgroups of $\Delta(2,n,n-1)$ , by Theorem 2.5 both $\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}$ are Fuchsian groups. $(iii)$ Consider the restriction

$$ \varphi\Big|_{\Gamma}\colon\Gamma\to G. $$

By the first isomorphism theorem, $G\simeq\Gamma/\operatorname{ker}\left(\varphi\Big|_{\Gamma}\right)$ , and since $\Gamma^{\prime}=\ker\varphi=\operatorname{ker}\left(\varphi\Big|_{\Gamma}\right)$ , we have $G\simeq\Gamma/\Gamma^{\prime}$ . Consequently, given that both $\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}$ are Fuchsian groups, by Corollary 2.2, it then follows that

$$ G\simeq\Gamma/\Gamma^{\prime}\simeq\operatorname{Mon}(\pi), $$

where $\pi\colon\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash\mathbb{H}\to\Gamma\backslash\mathbb{H}$ . ∎

#### Remark 3.3.

One may observe that the homomorphism $\varphi$ in Section 3.2 is really a projection map $F_{2}/N\to F_{2}/K$ , where $N$ and $K$ are the normal closures of the relations defining $\Delta(2,n,n-1)$ and $S_{n}$ , respectively. Hence, the kernel of this map can be explicitly computed as $K/N$ .
